title: A year on Mars, from its distance alone

intent.goal: Show that a planet's year follows from the size of its orbit (Kepler's third law), using Mars.
intent.takeaway: Farther from the Sun means a longer and slower trip: T = a^(3/2).
intent.hook: You can work out how long a Martian year is with one number.

science.model: two-body orbits round the Sun, solved from Kepler's equation
caveats: Orbits are drawn in one plane with their closest points in the same direction; the real orbits are tilted and turned relative to each other.
The Sun and planets are not drawn to scale.
Both planets start at their closest point to the Sun; this is not a real date.

music.mood: wide, slow synth pad with a soft pulse

sfx: a quiet tick each time Earth completes a lap

camera.moves: none: flat 2D view from above the orbits

timeline.visual: Sun, two faint orbits, Earth and Mars at their start points. Title.
Both planets move with their true speeds for exactly one Mars orbit, leaving bright trails. A readout counts Earth years and laps.

timeline.purpose: Give the rule and the check.
timeline.visual: Planets rest. The card shows the third law with Mars's numbers and the comparison with the measured period.

subtitle.text: worked out from its distance alone

readout.text: {t} Earth years  ·  Earth {e} laps  ·  Mars {m} laps

c1_heading.text: Mars orbits 1.524 times farther out than Earth

c1_note.text: A longer path, travelled more slowly. Both orbits are solved from Kepler's equation.

c2_heading.text: Kepler's third law (T in years, a in Earth distances)

c2_note.text: That is 687 days. Measured: 687 days. They agree within 0.01%.
